Continuing my project of representing textbook problems, I have this proof in progress:

import Mathlib.Data.Set.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Card

section
example {α : Type*} [Mul α] (G : Set α) [hG_fin : Finite G]
    {g : α} (h_nonempty : g ∈ G)
    (h_closed : ∀ {a b : α}, a ∈ G → b ∈ G → a * b ∈ G)
    (h_assoc : ∀ (a b c : α), (a * b) * c = a * (b * c))
    (lcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, x * a = x * b → a = b)
    (rcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, a * x = b * x → a = b)
    : Group G := by
  have h_lid : ∃ e ∈ G, ∀ x ∈ G, e * x = x := by
    let s := {y * g | y ∈ G}
    -- Since g ∈ G, s ⊆ G.
    have hs : s ⊆ G := by
      sorry
    -- There is a bijection f : s → G
    let f := fun y ↦ y * g
    have f_bij : Set.BijOn f G s := by
      sorry
    -- A finite set in bijection with a subset of itself is equal to that subset:
    have _finiteness_certificate_G := Fintype.ofFinite G
    have _finiteness_certificate_s := (Set.Finite.subset hG_fin hs).fintype
    have h1 := Fintype.ofEquiv_card f_bij.equiv
    have s_eq_G : s = G := by
      apply Set.eq_of_subset_of_card_le hs
      apply le_of_eq
      exact h1.symm -- doesn't work; h1 displays identically to the goal but is typed... differently?

    sorry
  sorry
end

At the line exact h1.symm, the goal is Fintype.card ↑G = Fintype.card ↑s, and h1 is Fintype.card ↑s = Fintype.card ↑G. I'm not doing anything underhanded - I've proven that the sets have equal cardinality, and I want to use that, along with the statement s⊆Gs \subseteq Gs⊆G, to prove that the sets themselves are equal.

I take it that my proof that the cardinalities are equal is... incompatible somehow... with Set.eq_of_subset_of_card_le. But why?

use docs#Fintype.card_congr instead of docs#Fintype.ofEquiv_card, which is specifically about docs#Fintype.ofEquiv (not sure why they don't have a description of this in the docstring like they do for docs#Fintype.card_ofSubsingleton and docs#Fintype.card_ofIsEmpty)

another strategy is to avoid Fintype altogether, as it puts you at risk of running into these instance mismatch issues

consider using Set.Finite with docs#Nat.card_congr and docs#Set.Finite.eq_of_subset_of_card_le (unless computability is important)

I'll explain what's going on here.

docs#Fintype.card has a Fintype instance argument (the [Fintype α] part of the definition). So when you see this:

Fintype.card ↑G = Fintype.card ↑s

what you're really looking at is:

Fintype.card ↑G Fintype_G_instance = Fintype.card ↑s Fintype_s_instance

If you look at the definition of docs#Fintype.ofEquiv_card, you'll notice that the theorem has a [Fintype α] argument but not a [Fintype β] argument... why is that? It's because this theorem constructs its own Fintype instance for β (specifically, it uses Fintype.ofEquiv). The goal, on the other hand, uses those finiteness certificate instances that you defined. That's why your proof appears to be "incompatible" with the goal: the Fintype instances aren't equal.

(Fintype.card_congr pulls in Fintype instances from the context for both sides of the equation, which is why Aaron suggested using that instead.)

Prop-valued classes, such as Finite, don't run into this problem because of proof irrelevance... any two proofs that a set is Finite are equal to each other, regardless of how they were constructed. Fintype is Type-valued (it's "data"), so two different Fintype instances are not equal unless they were constructed the same way. The benefit of Fintype being data is that it's computable, but the drawback is problems like the one you ran into here.
@Michael hope this helps

I don't know how well I can directly apply that, but I appreciate knowing it.

This ties in to some other problems I've had. The reason I was using Fintype.ofEquiv_card was that it had "equiv" in the name, which made it easier to find. Even if I'd noticed a theorem named card_congr, I wouldn't have seen it as worth investigating, because the name doesn't suggest anything about what it might be for. :face_with_diagonal_mouth:

Nat.card_congr has the same problem, but it also has the additional problem of being located in a completely different library, Mathlib.SetTheory.Cardinal.Finite as opposed to Mathlib.Data.Fintype.Card. (Relatedly: how do I predict whether what I want comes from Set.Finite or Finset?)

(I also note that the error messages from Lean always say "couldn't synthesize an instance of Fintype", even if the problem might be better addressed with a set-based approach, which pushes me toward looking for solutions to do with Fintype. I last encountered this while trying to apply Finset.prod to a Finite group. Which required a Fintype instance. In that case, I'm not sure how much better trying to implement a set-based approach would be, since Group acts on a type.)

For this problem, I did find docs#Set.BijOn.ncard_eq, which seemed like a good match, but my v4.28.0 project complained that there was no such identifier, and importing Mathlib.Data.Set.Card, which is where that theorem is described in the docs, didn't help.
@Michael I would recommend using https://leansearch.net and https://loogle.lean-lang.org if you're having trouble navigating Mathlib
(btw Finset.prod doesn't require a Fintype instance so I'm not sure what happened there)

For example, here's how to find Fintype.card_congr using Loogle:
https://loogle.lean-lang.org/?q=_+%E2%89%83+_%2C+Fintype.card+_+%3D+Fintype.card+_

@Matt Diamond 

import Mathlib

section
variable (G : Type*) [CommGroup G]

-- [Finite] is preferred for theorem statements,
--  "unless the statement requires [Fintype]."
-- ∏ notation does require [Fintype], so we put the assumption here.
example {x : G} [Fintype G] (hx : x = ∏ g : G, g) : x * x = 1 := by
  -- every inverse is unique, so {g | g ∈ G} = {g⁻¹ | g ∈ G}
  have hxinv : x = ∏ g : G, g⁻¹ := by
    rw [hx]
    apply Finset.prod_bijective (·⁻¹)
    · apply And.intro inv_injective inv_surjective
    · simp only [Finset.mem_univ, implies_true]
    · intro i hi; rw [inv_inv]
  -- do some rewriting to match the assumptions of Finset.prod_mul_prod_comm
  conv => lhs; lhs; rw [hx]; arg 2; ext g; rw [← mul_one g, ← id_eq g]
  conv => lhs; rhs; rw [hxinv]; arg 2; ext g; rw [← mul_one g⁻¹]
  rw [Finset.prod_mul_prod_comm id (fun a ↦ 1) (·⁻¹) (fun a ↦ 1)]
  conv => lhs; rw [one_mul]; lhs; arg 2; ext a; rw [id_eq, mul_inv_cancel]
  -- the product of a finite number of 1s is 1
  rw [Finset.prod_eq_one, mul_one]
  intro x hx; rfl
end

Deleting the [Fintype G] assumption produces a typing error: failed to synthesize instance of type class Fintype G. (And you get the same error if you have a [Finite G] assumption.)

(Providing Fintype there bothered me, because I saw the note that said "always use Finite", but when I asked about it here, the response was "it also says 'unless you need Fintype', which is true for your example.")

Following up on the original example, the goal (my goal, not "the goal" in lean) is to use the assumptions stated for the example to show that there is a group structure on G (where G is a Set of some other type α) via docs#Group.ofLeftAxioms .

I have successfully proven:

  1. h_lid : ∃ e ∈ G, ∀ x ∈ G, e * x = x
  2. e : α := h_lid.choose
  3. he : e ∈ G
  4. h_linv : ∀ x ∈ G, ∃ y ∈ G, y * x = e

And I've also defined:

have one_G : One G := ⟨e, he⟩
have inv_G : Inv G := ⟨fun (x : ↑G) ↦ by
  have h1 := (h_linv x x.property)
  let y := h1.choose
  have h2 := h1.choose_spec
  exact ⟨y, h2.1⟩⟩

I feel that this should be sufficient to invoke Group.ofLeftAxioms to show a group structure on G, but I'm getting buried in typing errors. Are there theorems somewhere that let you apply group structure to Sets?
It's hard to say without a #mwe or knowing what the errors are

the reason for h_assoc_in_G_specifically, for example, is that if I attempt to pass h_assoc, I get an error saying that h_assoc works for variables of type α, but the argument to Group.ofLeftAxioms G needs to work for variables of type ↑G.
@Ruben Van de Velde

Re your Fintype questions: You could state it like this

example {x : G} [Finite G] (hx : x = ∏ᶠ g : G, g) : x * x = 1 := by

if you'd rather stick with Finite.
Re your example above: ⊢ Group ↑G is not a true-false statement so you should not really be "proving" it in tactic mode -- it is not something you prove, it is data.

import Mathlib.Data.Finite.Card

section

def G_mul (h_closed : ∀ {a b : α}, a ∈ G → b ∈ G → a * b ∈ G)
    (x y : G) : G :=
  ⟨x.1 * y.1, h_closed x.2 y.2⟩

def G_one (hG_fin : Finite G)
    {g : α} (h_nonempty : g ∈ G)
    (h_closed : ∀ {a b : α}, a ∈ G → b ∈ G → a * b ∈ G)
    (h_assoc : ∀ (a b c : α), (a * b) * c = a * (b * c))
    (lcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, x * a = x * b → a = b)
    (rcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, a * x = b * x → a = b) : G :=
  sorry -- needs a definition, don't use tactic mode until you start on the proof

def G_inv (hG_fin : Finite G)
    {g : α} (h_nonempty : g ∈ G)
    (h_closed : ∀ {a b : α}, a ∈ G → b ∈ G → a * b ∈ G)
    (h_assoc : ∀ (a b c : α), (a * b) * c = a * (b * c))
    (lcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, x * a = x * b → a = b)

    {g : α} (h_nonempty : g ∈ G)
    (h_closed : ∀ {a b : α}, a ∈ G → b ∈ G → a * b ∈ G)
    (h_assoc : ∀ (a b c : α), (a * b) * c = a * (b * c))
    (lcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, x * a = x * b → a = b)
    (rcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, a * x = b * x → a = b)
    : Group G where
  mul := G_mul G h_closed
  mul_assoc := sorry
  one := sorry -- fill in from above
  one_mul := sorry
  mul_one := sorry
  inv := sorry -- fill in from above

You seem to want to "do everything in one go" but this is not really the best way to formalize.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Re your example above: ⊢ Group ↑G is not a true-false statement so you should not really be "proving" it in tactic mode -- it is not something you prove, it is data.

I don't think this makes sense. Compare

have mul_G_specifically : Mul G := ⟨fun (x₁ x₂ : ↑G) ↦ by
    have h1 : x₁.val * x₂.val ∈ G := by
      apply h_closed x₁.property x₂.property
    exact ⟨x₁.val * x₂, h1⟩⟩

Here, the instance of Mul G is constructed from a function that multiplies two terms of type ↑G. The function is defined in tactic mode (↦ by), because that's much more intelligible than doing it the other way. But that makes no difference; tactic mode has no special relationship to Props. It's just a different way to write the same computations.

I understand that they seem the same, but the output of tactic mode is often messier than the equivalent term mode version, and this can cause problems when you're trying to prove things about the term you just defined.

I'm not sure I agree that defining it in tactic mode is more intelligible than the term mode version. I know that figuring out a concise term mode version can be difficult, so I get the temptation to reach for tactics. In this case, however, the term mode version of your example is pretty simple:

have mul_G_specifically : Mul G := ⟨
  fun (x₁ x₂ : ↑G) ↦ ⟨x₁.val * x₂.val, h_closed x₁.property x₂.property⟩
⟩
also, if you want to define everything in a tactic block, you should use let when defining your typeclasses (One, Inv, and Mul) because have erases the definitions

have is basically a way of saying "I have a term of this type, but the term itself doesn't really matter" (which is the case when you're dealing with proofs of propositions), but the specific terms do matter when it comes to the algebraic operations you're defining
I agree that you can define data in tactic mode if you understand exactly what the tactics are doing and the terms they'll produce. It's also a recipe for disaster if you don't.

I got Group.ofLeftAxioms to work. (Thanks, Matt Diamond!) There is an issue (I think it's still a typing issue) that I remain curious about:

For each branch of ofLeftAxioms, I have to transfer the proof about ↑G to a proof about α via Subtype.ext. In every case, I can use conv to rewrite the goal as something less alien.

However, in two cases (left identity and left inverse), that rewriting is cosmetic and the proof will compile whether it's present or not. In the other case, associativity, the rewriting is not cosmetic and the proof won't work without it. In all cases, I'm using conv's change tactic, which as far as I understand it will only perform replacements that are "definitionally equal".

I'd like to understand more about why I have to do the rewriting manually for associativity, but not for the other two subgoals.

import Mathlib.Algebra.Group.MinimalAxioms
import Mathlib.Data.Finite.Card
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Card

section

variable {α : Type*} [Mul α] (G : Set α)

noncomputable example (hG_fin : Finite G)
    {g : α} (h_nonempty : g ∈ G)
    (h_closed : ∀ {a b : α}, a ∈ G → b ∈ G → a * b ∈ G)
    (h_assoc : ∀ (a b c : α), (a * b) * c = a * (b * c))
    (lcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, x * a = x * b → a = b)
    (rcancel : ∀ {a b x : α}, a * x = b * x → a = b)
    : Group G := by
  have h_lid : ∃ e ∈ G, ∀ x ∈ G, e * x = x := by
    sorry -- proof works; stubbed out
  let e := h_lid.choose
  have ⟨he, he'⟩ : e ∈ G ∧ ∀ x ∈ G, e * x = x := by
    apply h_lid.choose_spec
  have h_linv : ∀ x ∈ G, ∃ y ∈ G, y * x = e := by
    sorry -- proof works; stubbed out
  let one_G : One G := ⟨e, he⟩
  let inv_G : Inv G := ⟨fun (x : ↑G) ↦ by
    have h1 := (h_linv x x.property)
    let y := h1.choose
    have h2 := h1.choose_spec
    exact ⟨y, h2.1⟩⟩
  let mul_G_specifically : Mul G := ⟨fun (x₁ x₂ : ↑G) ↦ by
    have h1 : x₁.val * x₂.val ∈ G := by
      apply h_closed x₁.property x₂.property
    exact ⟨x₁.val * x₂, h1⟩⟩
  -- ofLeftAxioms doesn't include closure, because the requirement for
  --  a [Mul] instance means that * is closed by definition.
  apply Group.ofLeftAxioms
  -- * is associative, considered while restricted to G
  · intro a b c
    ext
    conv => lhs; change ↑a * ↑b * ↑c    -- can't be commented out
    conv => rhs; change ↑a * (↑b * ↑c)  -- can't be commented out
    rw [← h_assoc]
  -- 1 (e) is a left identity for G
  · intro a
    ext
    --conv => change e * a.val = a.val
    apply he' a.val a.property
  -- every element of G has a left inverse
  · intro a
    ext
    let h1 := h_linv a.1 a.2
    --let y := h1.choose
    --conv => change y * ↑a = e
    apply h1.choose_spec.2
end

It's because apply also sees through definitional equality and rw doesn't. Indeed, this also works:

  · intro a b c
    ext
    -- conv => lhs; change ↑a * ↑b * ↑c    -- can't be commented out
    -- conv => rhs; change ↑a * (↑b * ↑c)  -- can't be commented out
    -- rw [← h_assoc]
    apply h_assoc
This makes proofs using apply this way or change less robust to changes in the definitions and thus best avoided in code that should be maintainable
What's an example of a problem that a proof with apply will experience when a definition changes that the same proof with rewrite wouldn't?

When you use rw, you are being very explicit about what should change to what. So, a change in definition is likely to make the rw break, but at least you will know exactly what went wrong.

With apply, you are being more opaque as to what kind of definitional equality you are exploiting. This means that breaking code may be trickier to fix.

Of course, when things break it could go either way, but generally being explicit and intentional about definitionally equalities tends to be easier to maintain.
